newsitem.title: UK: Venezuela not to waste oil riches on wages-ministe.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela not to waste oil riches on wages-ministe.

text.p: Venezuela said on Wednesday that windfall oil revenues swelling its hard currency reserves would not blunt its resolve to reform despite mounting demands for public sector wage rises and stubborn inflation.
Last April the country embarked on a tough reform programme designed to slash triple-digit inflation and open its economy to foreign participation.
It hiked gasoline prices by 500 percent, raised taxes and removed controls on currency trading. Two key banks were privatised.

"These are irreversible changes, and we have put into the equation some instruments to guarantee that Venezuela doesn't have the same volatility it had in the past," said Luis Matos Azocar, Venezuela's minister of finance, on a two-day official visit to Britain.

The oil-rich Latin American country has banked unexpected profits since oil prices started on an upward trajectory in August. Its foreign reserves rose to about $15 billion from around $9 billion in April.
But some analysts fear a repeat of the country's 1990-91 performance when it backtracked on reform when oil prices rose following the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait.

Matos said a macro-economic stabilisation fund and a debt rescue fund would absorb the windfall revenues from higher oil prices and privatisation, allowing Venezuela to shore itself up against leaner times.
He said the debt rescue fund will begin in February with some $800 million, gaining an expected $3 billion from the privatisation of its aluminium and steel concerns in the second half of 1997.
"The aluminium and steel privatisation proceeds have not been written into the 1997 budget -- they are calculated at about $3 billion and will go into the rescue fund," Matos said.

Venezuela has said it intends to retire some of its Brady debt, but Matos conceded this was more difficult now due to the steep rise in Venezuelan debt prices -- now trading at around 90 percent of face value from 45 percent before April.
He said Venezuela intends to reduce its debt burden to 25 percent of government revenues by 1998 from 40 percent at present, but declined to comment on how this could be achieved.
"It is still a good opportunity, but it is not as good as it was when it was at 45 percent," he said, referring to the possibility of a Brady buy-back. "We will have to look for some other approach."
Venezuela's debt stock totals about 41 percent of GDP, he said.
Matos said Venezuela was aiming at GDP growth of at least 4.0 percent this year and was sticking to an inflation target of 25 percent, down from 103 percent in 1996.
"The tendency is that we are defeating inflation. In 1997 our goal is to have 25 percent; in 1998 our goal is to have inflation below 10 percent," Matos said.
"This is the strategy and all our economic and monetary policies are working in that direction," he added.
However many analysts believe the 25 percent inflation target is unrealistic, given mounting wage demands which will test the government's resolve.

Workers at telecoms firm CANTV are asking for wage rises of 120 percent pressures to compensate for last year's high levels and earlier this month the government gave striking doctors a 164 percent rise.
But Matos said the doctors' deal would not increase pressure on the 1997 budget.
"We expect no modification of the 1.3 billion bolivars (for public sector wage rises) in the budget," Matos told reporters. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
